title: Lesson 13 - A2.1.8 Cloud & IoT Vulnerabilities
subject: Information Technology
bigQuestion: How can cloud and IoT devices create new security risks?

head: Cloud computing
IoT (Internet of Things)
rows: Meaning
Using storage, software or processing power over the internet, instead of keeping everything on your own equipment
Everyday devices that connect to a network or the internet to collect, send or receive data
Examples
Microsoft 365, Google Drive, Amazon Web Services, OneDrive
Smart speakers, CCTV cameras, smart doorbells, fitness trackers, smart thermostats, sensors, smart TVs
Business example
A business stores customer files in a cloud service instead of on its own server
A company uses smart CCTV cameras that can be viewed remotely
Why it matters for security
The organisation has less direct physical control over where its data and systems are
Devices are small, cheap and low-powered, so they often have fewer security features than a normal computer

sections.heading: Cloud vulnerabilities

head: Vulnerability
The problem
Reduce the risk
rows: Incorrect security settings
Default settings make setup easy but may not be secure enough, e.g. cloud storage accidentally shared so outsiders can open sensitive files
Check and configure settings properly. A secure cloud service can still be insecure if it's set up wrong
Third-party access
Provider administrators, engineers and support staff may have technical access, so the organisation must trust the provider. What if the provider's security is weak?
Choose a trustworthy provider and manage third-party risk (TPRM)
Data moving over the internet
Data travels between the organisation, the internet and the provider, so it could be intercepted, stolen or changed
Encryption and secure connections such as HTTPS and VPNs

points: Remember: data needs protecting when it's stored AND when it's being transferred

diagram.alt: Data travels from your organisation across the internet to a cloud provider. Using HTTPS or a VPN encrypts it in transit, so an attacker who intercepts it can't read it. At the cloud provider, stored data should also be encrypted and the security settings configured correctly.
diagram.caption: Protect data when it is stored AND when it is being transferred.

sections.heading: IoT vulnerabilities

head: Vulnerability
Example / risk
Prevention
rows: Default passwords
A smart camera keeps its default login; an attacker finds it online, tries the manufacturer's default and gets into the camera or its settings
Change default passwords to strong, unique ones
Weak or no encryption
A device sends data across the network without suitable encryption; an attacker intercepts it, so information is exposed or changed
Secure communications and appropriate encryption
Lack of updates
The manufacturer doesn't provide patches, or the user doesn't install them, so the vulnerability stays and can be targeted for a long time
Install updates; replace devices that no longer get them
Insecure control interfaces
A camera's online control panel (app, website or cloud dashboard) has weak authentication; an attacker takes control and changes settings
Strong authentication on apps, websites and dashboards
Poor network security
Devices installed by people outside the IT team, with no checks; they may not work with the firewall, may not be monitored, and could be a route into the wider network
IT checks every device before it connects, and monitors it
Always listening
Smart speakers, doorbells, meeting assistants and cameras record continuously; if compromised, they could be used for eavesdropping or surveillance
Keep them out of rooms where confidential information is discussed

points: Key point: every device connected to a network is another potential entry point
Remember: a device can work normally and still be vulnerable

sections.heading: Exam method
sections.text: Don't just name the vulnerability. Your slides' exam tip is to build each point as a chain:
points: Explain the risk: how an attacker could exploit it
Explain the impact: what could happen to the organisation or its data
Suggest a control: what would reduce the risk
It's the same idea as Lesson 9's Cause → Risk → Impact → Response chain

sections.heading: Worked scenario: cameras, doorbells, speakers and cloud
sections.text: The slides' scenario: a business installed 20 smart cameras, 10 smart doorbells, smart speakers in meeting rooms and cloud storage, quickly, and some still use original settings. Here's one possible answer (mine, so try it first):

head: Vulnerability
Risk
Prevention
rows: Cameras and doorbells still on default passwords
Attackers find them online and log in with the manufacturer's default, viewing or switching off cameras
Change to strong, unique passwords
Smart speakers in meeting rooms (always listening)
If compromised, used to eavesdrop on confidential meetings
Remove them from meeting rooms or switch microphones off
Cloud storage on default settings
Files accidentally shared publicly, so sensitive documents are exposed
Check and configure sharing and access settings
Devices installed quickly without IT checks
Not monitored or behind the firewall, giving a route into the wider network
IT checks, monitoring and keeping devices updated

keyIdea: Cloud services move data and control to a third party over the internet, so wrong settings, provider access and data in transit become risks. IoT devices are cheap and connected, so default passwords, weak encryption, missing updates, insecure apps, unchecked network connections and always-on microphones all create new entry points.
flashcards: Cloud computing
Using storage, software or processing power over the internet instead of on your own equipment.
Cloud examples
Microsoft 365, Google Drive, Amazon Web Services, OneDrive.
Cloud security issue
The organisation has less direct physical control over where its data and systems are stored.
Incorrect security settings (cloud)
Default or wrong settings, e.g. storage that lets outsiders see sensitive files.
Third-party access
Provider administrators, engineers and support staff may have technical access to your systems and data.
TPRM
Third-party risk management: checking and managing the risks of relying on outside providers.
Data in transit
Data moving between the organisation, the internet and the provider. It could be intercepted, stolen or changed.
VPN
Virtual private network: a secure, encrypted connection over the internet.
Stored AND transferred
Data needs protecting both when it's stored and when it's moving.
IoT
Internet of Things: everyday devices that connect to a network to collect, send or receive data.
Why IoT is weaker
Devices are small, cheap and low-powered, so they often have fewer security features.
Default password
The username and password a device ships with. Attackers can guess or look them up.
Weak or no encryption (IoT)
Data sent without proper protection can be intercepted, read or changed.
Lack of updates (IoT)
No patches from the maker, or not installed, so a known vulnerability can be targeted for a long time.
Control interface
The app, website or cloud dashboard used to control an IoT device. Weak authentication lets attackers take over.
Poor network security (IoT)
Devices connected without IT checks may not be monitored or firewalled: a route into the network.
Entry point
Every device connected to a network is another possible way in.
Always listening
Devices with microphones or cameras that record continuously. If compromised, they enable eavesdropping.
Point → Risk → Impact → Control
The slides' exam method: name it, how it's exploited, what happens, how to reduce it.

quiz.q: Which of these is an IoT device?
quiz.e: IoT devices connect to a network or the internet to send or receive data.

quiz.q: Where might your photos, documents or messages be stored online?
o: In cloud storage such as Google Drive or OneDrive
quiz.e: Cloud storage keeps files on a provider's servers, accessed over the internet.

quiz.q: What could happen if someone hacked a smart camera or smart speaker?
o: They could watch or listen in
quiz.e: Always-on cameras and microphones can be used for surveillance or eavesdropping.

quiz.q: Why should you change the default password on a new device?
o: Attackers can guess or look up default passwords
quiz.e: Manufacturers' default logins are often published online.

o: Using storage, software or processing power over the internet
quiz.e: Instead of keeping everything on your own equipment, you use a provider's.

quiz.q: Why does using the cloud change an organisation's security?
o: It has less direct physical control over where its data is stored
quiz.e: The data sits with an external provider.

quiz.q: A company accidentally sets its cloud storage so anyone with the link can open sensitive files. Which vulnerability?
quiz.e: A secure cloud service can still become insecure if configured wrongly.

quiz.q: Why can using a third-party cloud provider create a security risk?
o: The provider's staff may have access, so you must trust their security
quiz.e: If the provider's security is weak, your data is at risk.

quiz.q: How can data moving to and from the cloud be protected?
o: Encryption and secure connections like HTTPS and VPNs
quiz.e: Protect data in transit as well as at rest.

quiz.q: Why do IoT devices often have fewer security features?
o: They're designed to be small, cheap and low-powered
quiz.e: Limited power and cost mean less built-in security.

quiz.q: Why can an IoT device be a security risk even if it's working normally?
o: It may have unpatched vulnerabilities that attackers can target
quiz.e: A device can work fine while still being vulnerable.

quiz.q: A smart camera's online control panel has weak login security, and an attacker changes its settings. Which vulnerability?
quiz.e: Apps, websites and dashboards that control devices need strong authentication.

quiz.q: A member of staff plugs a smart speaker into the office network without telling IT. What's the main risk?
o: It isn't checked or monitored and could be a route into the network
It will play music too loudly
quiz.e: Every connected device is another potential entry point.

quiz.q: A company has 100 IoT devices that haven't had updates for years. What should it consider?
o: Doing nothing, as they still work
Replacing or updating them, and separating them from sensitive systems
quiz.e: Unpatched devices leave known vulnerabilities open for a long time.

quiz.q: Would you want an always-listening device in a room where confidential business information is discussed?
o: No, if compromised it could be used to eavesdrop
Only if it's switched to loud
quiz.e: Keep always-listening devices out of confidential spaces.

quiz.q: A smart device sends data across the network without encryption, and an attacker intercepts it. What could happen?
o: Information could be exposed or changed
quiz.e: Weak or no encryption means intercepted data can be read or altered.

apply.title: Spot the cloud or IoT risk
apply.intro: Pick the vulnerability or the best prevention for each situation.

items.task: A new smart doorbell still uses 'admin / admin' as its login.
o: Default password: change to a strong, unique one
items.e: Default logins are easy for attackers to find and try.

items.task: A company's cloud folder of payroll files is set to 'anyone with the link can view'.
items.e: Wrong settings can expose data even on a secure cloud service.

items.task: Engineers at the cloud provider can technically reach a company's stored data.
o: Third-party access: choose a trusted provider and manage third-party risk
items.e: The organisation must trust the provider's people and security.

items.task: Staff upload files to the cloud from home over public Wi-Fi with no protection.
o: Data in transit: use encryption, HTTPS and a VPN
items.e: Data moving over the internet could be intercepted, stolen or changed.

items.task: A fitness tracker sends health data to its app without encryption.
items.e: Intercepted data could be read or changed. Use secure communications.

items.task: A manufacturer stopped releasing updates for a model of smart camera three years ago, but the cameras still work.
o: Fully secure because they still work
items.e: A device can work normally while being vulnerable.

items.task: Someone logs in to a smart thermostat's web dashboard using a weak password and changes the office heating.
items.e: Weak authentication on the control interface lets attackers take control.

items.task: The marketing team plugs a smart TV into the office network without telling IT.
o: Poor network security: it's an unchecked entry point
items.e: IT should check and monitor every connected device.

items.task: A smart speaker sits in the boardroom where takeover plans are discussed.
items.e: If compromised, it could be used to listen to confidential meetings.

items.task: Which is the BEST answer structure for an 'explain' question on cloud or IoT risks?
items.e: That's the slides' exam tip: don't just name it.

items.task: Which TWO places must data be protected when using the cloud?
o: When stored and when being transferred
items.e: Data needs protecting at rest AND in transit.

items.task: Why are IoT devices described as extra 'entry points'?
o: Each connected device is another possible way into the network
items.e: More connected devices means more ways in.

exam.q: 1. Identify two vulnerabilities associated with IoT devices.
pts: Any one: default passwords / weak or no encryption / lack of updates
A second: insecure control interfaces / poor network security / always-listening microphones or cameras
exam.tip: From your slides' exam practice. "Identify" = name them, no need to explain.

exam.q: 2. Explain how incorrect security settings could create a security risk when using cloud computing.
pts: Cloud services often use default settings to make setup easy
but these may not be secure enough, e.g. storage configured so people outside the organisation can open files
so sensitive data could be viewed, copied or leaked by unauthorised people
A secure service can become insecure if configured wrongly, so settings must be checked and configured properly
exam.tip: From your slides' exam practice. Point → risk → impact → control.

exam.q: 3. Explain why using a third-party cloud provider can create a security risk for an organisation.
pts: People outside the organisation, such as the provider's administrators, engineers and support staff, may have technical access to its systems and data
so the organisation has to trust the provider, and if the provider's security is weak, its data is at risk
exam.tip: Who has access + why that's a risk.

exam.q: 4. Explain why an IoT device can be a security risk even if it is working normally.
pts: It may contain software vulnerabilities that haven't been patched, because the maker stopped updates or they weren't installed
so attackers can keep targeting the known vulnerability for a long time without the user noticing

exam.q: 5. Explain how data could be at risk when it is moved to and from a cloud provider, and how this risk can be reduced.
pts: Data travels between the organisation, the internet and the cloud provider
so it could be intercepted, stolen or changed while being transferred
Reduce it with encryption and secure connections such as HTTPS and VPNs
exam.tip: Remember: protect data when stored AND when transferred.

exam.q: 6. A company has 100 IoT devices that have not received updates for several years. What should the company consider doing?
pts: Check whether updates are still available and install them
Replace devices that no longer receive updates
Until then, separate them from sensitive systems, monitor them, and make sure default passwords have been changed
exam.tip: From the plenary. Give practical actions, ideally ranked by urgency.

exam.sc: A business has installed 20 smart security cameras, 10 smart doorbells, smart speakers in its meeting rooms, and cloud storage for its business documents. The devices were installed quickly, and some are still using their original settings.
exam.q: 7. Identify four possible vulnerabilities in this business and, for each, explain the risk and a possible prevention.
pts: Vulnerability and risk 1, e.g. cameras and doorbells still on default passwords, so attackers can log in and view or disable them
Prevention 1: change to strong, unique passwords
Vulnerability and risk 2, e.g. smart speakers in meeting rooms are always listening and could be used to eavesdrop
Prevention 2: remove them from meeting rooms or switch microphones off
Vulnerability and risk 3, e.g. cloud storage on default settings could expose business documents to outsiders
Prevention 3: check and configure the sharing and access settings
Vulnerability and risk 4, e.g. devices installed quickly without IT checks, so they're unmonitored entry points / not updated
Prevention 4: IT checks, monitoring, firewall rules and installing updates
exam.tip: This is the slides' scenario task. 2 marks per vulnerability: name it and explain the risk, then a matching prevention.

exam.sc: A business uses cloud storage and several internet-connected security cameras.
exam.q: 8. Explain the security risks the business should consider and how these risks could be reduced.
pts: Cloud risk: incorrect settings could let outsiders see sensitive files. Reduce by configuring and checking settings
Cloud risk: third-party access, since the provider's staff may reach data. Reduce by choosing a trusted provider and managing third-party risk
Cloud risk: data intercepted in transit. Reduce with encryption, HTTPS and VPNs
Camera risk: default passwords or insecure control apps let attackers view or switch off cameras. Reduce with strong, unique passwords and secure authentication
Camera risk: no updates or unchecked network connection, giving a route into the network. Reduce by updating, monitoring and firewalling the cameras
Impact explained, e.g. confidential data leaked, or security cameras disabled so the building is exposed
exam.tip: From your slides' exam practice. For 6 marks, cover BOTH the cloud and the cameras, and pair each risk with a control.
